item.title: Tavua's Nasivi River seepage issue rectified a year after concerns raised
item.description: A year after concerns were raised about alleged waste discharge into the Nasivi River in Tavua, the Water Authority of Fiji says the issue has been rectified following work with the Tavua Town Council. The authority says investigations found that an improper septic system was causing seepage into the river, and the problem was fixed earlier this month to stop the seepage.
item.content:encoded:
A year after concerns were raised about alleged waste discharge into the Nasivi River in Tavua, the Water Authority of Fiji says the issue has been rectified following work with the Tavua Town Council.

The authority says investigations found that an improper septic system was causing seepage into the river, and the problem was fixed earlier this month to stop the seepage.

However, we have sent further questions to WAF, to confirm whether the discharge was from Tavua Hospital.

The issue was first raised during the Fijian Media Association’s ‘Meet the Public and the Press’ session at the Golden Event Centre in Tavua in October last year.

Two Tavua residents, including Chair of the Land-Owning Unit for Tavua, Tevita Ralulu, alleged that Tavua Hospital was discharging waste into the Nasivi River.

When questioned by fijivillage News at the time about whether an assessment had begun, the late Permanent Secretary for Health Jemesa Tudravu said his team had not received anything on the matter at the time.

Water Authority of Fiji Chief Executive Officer Seru Soderberg also addressed the issue during the session, stressing that such discharges were illegal under environmental laws.

Soderberg later confirmed to fijivillage News that a team had visited the site on Friday, October 17th, 2025, to conduct tests.

The Water Authority of Fiji says the issue has now been resolved following its work with the Tavua Town Council.

item.title: Fiji must address HIV and drug crisis while ensuring ordinary iTaukei voices are heard
item.description: Fiji must urgently address the growing concerns over HIV and drug-related issues, with stronger community support and greater efforts to reach those affected. This was highlighted by Founder of Drug Free World Fiji and People’s First Party proposed candidate, Kalesi Toga Volatabu, who resides in Wailevu, during the Constitution (Amendment) Bill consultation.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji must urgently address the growing concerns over HIV and drug-related issues, with stronger community support and greater efforts to reach those affected.

This was highlighted by Founder of Drug Free World Fiji and People’s First Party proposed candidate, Kalesi Toga Volatabu, who resides in Wailevu, during the Constitution (Amendment) Bill consultation.

Volatabu raises concerns about the country's HIV and drug crisis, questioning who is speaking for the affected communities and what more needs to be done to address the gaps.

She says the proposed constitutional changes must consider the needs of ordinary iTaukei people, particularly those whose voices are often not heard in decision-making.

Volatabu points out that, according to the figures she cited during her submission, iTaukei people account for 90 percent of new HIV cases, questioning what is being done to address the situation and how communities can be better supported.

She says there is a disconnection between decision-makers and people on the ground, stressing the need to understand the challenges communities are facing and respond to their needs.

Volatabu says she is not against having a constitution, as every country needs one, but believes people must be given sufficient time to understand and consider the proposed changes.

She also raises concerns about the proposed constitutional role and powers of the Great Council of Chiefs, questioning whether the arrangements would ensure ordinary iTaukei people are adequately represented and able to hold decision-makers accountable.

Volatabu says the abilities, skills and capacity of those entrusted with significant powers must be considered, along with whether they will speak for everyone rather than a select group.

She stresses that iTaukei women must also have a stronger voice in the constitutional review process, saying their experiences and priorities differ depending on their age, disability, income and education.

Volatabu notes that only one woman was present on the review platform during the consultation, raising concerns about the level of women's participation and representation.

She says more women must be given opportunities to contribute to decisions that affect them and their communities.

Volatabu also questions the short timeframe for the constitutional review, describing the 11-week consultation period as rushed.

She compares this with the 2013 Constitution review process, which she says took four years and received more than 7,000 submissions.

She says a constitution that governs the entire country must be fair and just for everyone, rather than being shaped only by influential people or the elite.

While welcoming the opportunity for the review team to meet people directly, Volatabu says more must be done to ensure communities across Fiji have the chance to participate and share their views.

She also questions the accountability of those appointed under the proposed arrangements, particularly in relation to the appointment of the President and Vice-President, stressing the need for proper checks and balances.

Volatabu further raises concerns about the iTaukei Land Trust Board, saying that although it is mandated to serve landowners, her experience on the ground has led her to question whether their interests are being prioritised over those of investors.

She says the role of the TLTB should be strengthened to ensure it remains focused on serving and protecting the interests of the people it represents.

Volatabu says the issue is not simply whether the Great Council of Chiefs should have a constitutional role, but whether any significant powers given to it would be balanced by clear guarantees that ordinary iTaukei people, particularly women, can participate in, understand and scrutinise decisions made in their name.

She warns that rushing constitutional changes risks making the process appear imposed rather than shared, saying people need sufficient time, accessible information and a genuine opportunity to influence the proposed changes before a referendum.

Volatabu says the views of the Great Council of Chiefs are important but cannot replace the voices of all iTaukei people or the wider population of Fiji.

She says she does not support Clause 2.7, Chapter 4 of the proposed Bill, which she believes gives significant powers to the Great Council of Chiefs without sufficient guarantees for ordinary iTaukei people to have their say.

Volatabu ended her submission with a clear message: “Nothing about us without us.”

item.title: Lautoka father raises safety concerns after daughter injured near children's park
item.description: A Lautoka resident is raising safety concerns about an exposed metal piece fixed into the pavement near the entrance of a children's park after his daughter injured her knee when she tripped and fell. Kamal Kant Prasad says the incident happened at around 4.30pm on Saturday as he was leaving the park with his daughter to go to his parked vehicle.
item.content:encoded:
A Lautoka resident is raising safety concerns about an exposed metal piece fixed into the pavement near the entrance of a children's park after his daughter injured her knee when she tripped and fell.

Kamal Kant Prasad says the incident happened at around 4.30pm on Saturday as he was leaving the park with his daughter to go to his parked vehicle.

Prasad says his daughter tripped and hurt her knee while walking along the footpath.

He says the exposed piece is the bottom portion used to secure a road sign into the concrete and is less than a foot tall.

Prasad is concerned that the hazard remains near the entrance of the children's park, which is visited daily by children and their parents.

He is calling for the relevant authorities to address the issue as soon as possible to prevent other children and members of the public from getting injured.

Meanwhile, Lautoka City Council Head of Services Shalend Singh says the Council was made aware of the exposed metal hazard this morning and has notified the Fiji Roads Authority to address the issue.

Singh says the signboard was installed by FRA but was later vandalised.

He says the Council is also compiling a list of safety hazards across the city, including exposed metal, exposed gully grating and open manhole lids, to bring to the attention of the relevant agencies.

item.title: A family legacy takes flight: Father and sons soar with Fiji Airways
item.description: A father's passion for aviation has become a family legacy, with his two sons following in his footsteps to proudly represent Fiji Airways in the skies. For more than four decades, Captain Ilaitia Caucau has dedicated his career to Fiji's national airline, and today, that same passion for flying lives on through his sons, Edwin and Isireli, who have built careers of their own in aviation.
item.content:encoded:
A father's passion for aviation has become a family legacy, with his two sons following in his footsteps to proudly represent Fiji Airways in the skies.

For more than four decades, Captain Ilaitia Caucau has dedicated his career to Fiji's national airline, and today, that same passion for flying lives on through his sons, Edwin and Isireli, who have built careers of their own in aviation.

Caucau says he officially joined the airline on 3rd January 1984, and after more than 42 years, he remains proud to be part of the Fiji Airways family.

His son Edwin now serves as a First Officer on Fiji Airways' Airbus A350 and A330 aircraft.

Edwin says aviation has been a lifelong dream, and growing up around aircraft made the decision to become a pilot an easy one.

His elder brother, Isireli, also pursued a career in aviation, beginning as a Twin Otter pilot with Fiji Link before joining Fiji Airways earlier this year as a Cruise Relief Pilot.

The brothers recall that aircraft were always part of their childhood.

From playing with toy planes to watching their father prepare for work, aviation was a constant presence in their lives.

They say watching their father put on his uniform and leave to fly around the world inspired them from a young age and helped shape their ambitions.

For Edwin, one of the most memorable moments of his career was sharing the flight deck with his father.

His first flight alongside Captain Caucau was to Hong Kong, an experience he describes as special and unforgettable.

While proud of his father's achievements as a pilot, Edwin says he is even more grateful for the role he has played as a parent, describing him as the best father in the world.

The Caucau family also regards Fiji Airways as the pinnacle of aviation in Fiji, with the airline representing the ultimate career goal for many aspiring pilots across the country.

Their story highlights dedication, family and a shared passion for flying, showing how a father's love for aviation has inspired the next generation to follow in his footsteps.

item.title: Sayed-Khaiyum raises concerns over social pension cuts, Kiran clarifies eligibility
item.description: Senior citizens who own basic household items such as a TV and a refrigerator are not automatically disqualified from receiving social pensions. This has been clarified by Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection, Sashi Kiran following comments made by former Attorney-General Aiyaz Sayed-Khaiyum that some older people had reportedly stopped receiving their pensions after being subjected
item.content:encoded:
Senior citizens who own basic household items such as a TV and a refrigerator are not automatically disqualified from receiving social pensions.

This has been clarified by Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection, Sashi Kiran following comments made by former Attorney-General Aiyaz Sayed-Khaiyum that some older people had reportedly stopped receiving their pensions after being subjected to asset tests.

In a recent interview, Sayed-Khaiyum said many people who used to receive social pensions were no longer receiving them.

He said many people in Fiji work as domestic helpers, roadside sellers and farmers, particularly in villages, but do not have access to the Fiji National Provident Fund (FNPF) because they have never worked in formal employment.

Sayed-Khaiyum said these people often have no retirement savings to rely on when they grow old.

He said the Social Pension Scheme initially provided $50 a month to people aged 70 and above who had never been members of the FNPF, before being expanded to cover those aged 65 and above, with payments increased to $100 a month.

Sayed-Khaiyum said he had been told that some older people in Lautoka were no longer receiving the assistance, despite previously being eligible.

He said some had reportedly undergone asset tests.

He added that because they own assets such as refrigetrators and television, they no longer get pension money.

In response, Kiran says the statements appear to confuse the Social Pension Scheme with the Family Assistance Scheme, which are separate programmes with different objectives, assessment processes and eligibility criteria.

She says eligible Fiji citizens aged 65 and above who do not receive an FNPF pension or another qualifying superannuation benefit may qualify for the Social Pension Scheme, subject to its eligibility requirements.

She says the scheme supported 51,784 senior citizens in 2023, with a budget of $57.4 million and 96 per cent budget utilisation.

For the 2025–2026 financial year, the Government increased the allocation to $82.06 million, supporting 59,918 recipients.

This represents an increase of 8,134 recipients, or 15.7 per cent, compared with 2023, alongside an additional $24.66 million in budget allocation.

Kiran says supporting vulnerable older persons, including former informal workers, subsistence farmers and market vendors with limited retirement savings, remains a priority.

She says more than 130,000 beneficiaries currently receive assistance through six major social welfare programmes.

It is also implementing reforms to improve transparency, accountability and service delivery, including reviewing social assistance programmes, improving poverty-targeting methods and strengthening verification processes.

She says anyone who believes their assistance has been stopped incorrectly should use its established grievance and review processes so their individual circumstances can be assessed.

She says eligibility decisions must follow the correct programme rules while ensuring public funds are administered responsibly.
